name: German Pennsylvania Colonial

revival_periods.note: Revived mainly as the 'Pennsylvania farmhouse' — fieldstone, pent eave, six-over-six sash — within the broader Colonial Revival rather than as a distinct named revival.

geography.hearth: the limestone country of Lancaster, Berks, Lebanon and Montgomery counties, Pennsylvania, settled from the Rhenish Palatinate and Switzerland after 1710

lineage.note: The framing tradition arrives intact and is built in Pennsylvania for a generation — the Golden Plough Tavern at York is half-timbered exactly as a Palatine house would be — before stone and log displace it.
Secondary: the habit of housing family, stock and crop under one steep roof survives in the Pennsylvania forebay bank barn more than in the dwelling.

Horizontal log construction reached the Delaware from New Sweden; the Germans adopted it, added V- and dovetail-notching and their own three-room plan, and made it the substrate of backcountry American building all the way to the Ozarks.
After about 1770 the Continental plan is progressively regularized behind a symmetrical five-bay Anglo front — the same house, wearing a different face.

description.short: The Continental stone and log house of the Palatine and Swiss migration: a three-room asymmetric plan around a central chimney serving a closed iron stove, built into a hillside wherever the ground allowed.
description.long:
Pennsylvania German building is the one colonial tradition organized around a heating technology rather than around a fireplace. The Palatine settler brought the five-plate jamb stove — a cast-iron box open only to the back, fed through a hole in the masonry from the kitchen hearth on the other side of the wall. This single device restructures the plan. The kitchen, the Küche, becomes a large room containing the only open fire; the stove-room, the Stube, sits on the other side of the chimney wall and is heated without smoke, soot, draught, or the need for anyone to tend it from within; and the Kammer, the sleeping chamber, tucks in behind the Stube. Three rooms, not two; asymmetric, not paired; and the chimney is central not because of thermal mass — the English reason — but because it is a service wall between a wet room and a dry one. The Anglo world took two hundred years to arrive at the same idea and called it a mechanical core.

The second organizing idea is the ground. Where the English built on a level platform and dug a cellar, the German builder set the house across a slope so that the lower storey opens at grade on the downhill side and is buried on the uphill side. This yields a cool, frost-free service level — often built directly over a spring, its water running out through an arched opening — reached from outside without stairs, and a dry principal floor entered from the upper grade. Two front doors on two different levels is the result, and it is the most reliable single tell of the tradition. Nothing about it is picturesque; it is a refrigerator, a root cellar and a dairy obtained for the cost of moving earth.

The walls are squared limestone or sandstone laid in lime mortar, eighteen to thirty inches thick, with dressed quoins and unusually large corner stones, or else horizontal log with V-notched or full-dovetail corners and mud-and-straw chinking. The roof is steep, forty-five to fifty degrees, framed with a liegender Stuhl — a leaning-post truss that stands clear of the attic floor and leaves the loft usable for grain. Windows are small, irregularly placed, and set where the room wanted them rather than where the elevation did; glass was expensive and the frontier was not safe. A pent roof, a shallow shed thirty to forty inches deep running across the facade at the second-floor line, keeps water off the wall and off anyone standing at the door.

Standing inside, the surprise is the silence and the dryness. A stone house with two-foot walls and small openings has a stillness that a timber house does not; the Stube in winter, warmed by a stove and lit by two small deep-set windows, is one of the most comfortable rooms colonial America produced, and it does this without a fire in sight. The tradition was negotiating against nothing more exotic than English fashion and English land law, and it lost the elevation while keeping the section — which is the pattern of nearly every immigrant building culture in America.

defining_characteristics: Asymmetric three-room Flurküchenhaus plan — Küche, Stube, Kammer — arranged around a central chimney mass, with no through passage
Central chimney serving an open cooking hearth in the kitchen and a closed five-plate jamb stove fed through the wall into the stove-room
Load-bearing squared stone (or V-notched horizontal log) walls 18–30 in thick, with oversized dressed quoins
Steep gable roof, 45–50 degrees, framed with a liegender Stuhl leaning-post truss over a usable loft
Small, irregularly spaced openings placed by interior need rather than by facade composition, with deep reveals
Vaulted or barrel-arched masonry cellar, frequently over a spring
Pent roof — a shallow shed 30–42 in deep at the second-floor line — across the facade or the gable end on eighteenth-century work
diagnostic_tells: A pent roof band across the facade at the second-floor line, with no posts under it
Windows that do not line up floor to floor, in a house otherwise carefully built — the plan is winning the argument with the elevation
Very large squared quoin stones against smaller coursed wall stone
A door at the gable end entering the kitchen, plus a second door on the facade — two entrances of unequal status
Interior: a flat chimney wall in the stove-room with a small square iron-lined aperture, the ghost of a jamb stove

distinguished_from.difference: Both are masonry, five-bay, steep-roofed and Pennsylvanian, and after 1780 they converge. The test is the plan and the openings: Georgian gives you a centre passage, a symmetrical rear elevation, aligned windows floor to floor, and a classical door surround. The German house gives you an asymmetric three-room plan, unaligned windows and a plain door with a hood.

Both build thick stone with steep roofs. The Dutch house has gable-end hearths, an open jambless fire, exposed anchor beams and a low plate; the German house has a central chimney with a closed stove, a liegender Stuhl truss and a banked lower storey.

The twentieth-century 'Pennsylvania farmhouse' takes the fieldstone, the pent eave and the six-over-six sash and applies them to a symmetrical centre-hall plan with aligned windows, a fireplace in every room, thin veneer stone and an attached garage. Wall thickness at the window reveal settles it: two feet of real masonry, or four inches of veneer.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The three-room plan module: a kitchen bay of 16–20 ft and a stove-room/chamber bay of the same total width, divided roughly 2:1, with the chimney on the dividing wall.
typical_ratios: Overall 28–38 ft × 22–30 ft, i.e. close to 4:3
Küche occupies 45–55% of the plan; Stube and Kammer share the remainder, Stube the larger
Wall thickness 18–30 in at the ground storey, reducing 2–4 in at the upper floor
Ceiling 7 ft 0 in – 8 ft 6 in; loft usable to the collar of the liegender Stuhl
Window opening ratio near 1:1.6, and total glazed area under 8% of wall area on early work
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Irregular on early work; a nominal three- or five-bay front emerges after 1770 but the door is often still off-centre because the chimney wall is.

massing_affinities.note: The nearest catalogued skeleton to the Flurküchenhaus, with the caveat that the German plan divides unequally and adds a third room.
The regularized post-1780 Pennsylvania farmhouse, sometimes with the distinctive paired central doors.
The log Einraumhaus of first settlement.
Growth by attaching kitchen and summer-kitchen wings along the contour.

constraints.statement: The chimney mass sits on the partition between kitchen and stove-room, serving an open hearth on one side and a closed stove aperture on the other. Moving it to the gable ends dissolves the plan type.
Roof pitch 10:12 to 12:12 (40–50 degrees). Pennsylvania German work does not go below 9:12; a 6:12 roof on fieldstone is a twentieth-century invention.

Pent roof, where used, projects 30–42 in at the second-floor line at a pitch of 25–35 degrees, is unsupported by posts, and returns 12–24 in around the corner. It is a pre-1780 feature; on later work it reads as revival.

test.note: Tests the pent roof's projection. Pitch (25-35deg) and corner return (12-24in) are the statement's other numeric claims and stay prose.

constraints.statement: Load-bearing wall 18–30 in of squared stone, with quoins 1.5 to 2.5 times the height of the field coursing. Window and door reveals must show the full wall depth; a flush jamb reveals a veneer.

test.note: Tests the wall thickness. The quoin-to-coursing size ratio is a niche one-off comparison and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Openings by period: small casements with iron hardware to c. 1760; nine-over-six sash c. 1760–1800; six-over-six after. Glazed area under 8% of wall area before 1770, under 12% after.

exemplars.name: Hans Herr House (1719 Museum)
exemplars.location: West Lampeter Township, Lancaster County, Pennsylvania
exemplars.note: The oldest building in Lancaster County and the canonical American Flurküchenhaus: squared sandstone with oversized quoins, three-room plan, central chimney, high steep roof, small casement openings.
exemplars.why: HABS calls it 'the oldest dwelling house in Lancaster County' and says it 'is important for its Germanic design'; it is the building every account of this tradition opens with, and its 37'-9" by 30-10" is the only plan dimension in the node that the survey states BAY BY BAY -- '(three bays) X ... (two bays)' -- so the front is not in doubt. CORRECTED 5 Sep 2026 by the cluster audit: this had read 'the only stated plan dimension the node has', which three sibling exemplars in this same file falsify -- the Golden Plough Tavern's 34' x 28'-5", the Troxell-Steckel House's 48 by 35 ft and the Bertolet-Herbein Cabin's 'approximately 20 feet by 30 feet'. The depth is printed 30-10" and the foot mark is an OCR loss; the measurement record marks it as a reading.

exemplars.name: Golden Plough Tavern
exemplars.note: Half-timbered Fachwerk with brick nogging, built as a Palatine builder would have built at home — the framing tradition before stone displaced it.
exemplars.why: The Fachwerk half of the tradition in a federal survey that calls it 'the only remaining example of half-timber construction, which was widely used during the early period of the region's settlement', with 34 by 28'-5" and a flared eave stated on the same form.

exemplars.name: Schifferstadt
exemplars.note: Built by Elias Bruner of the Palatinate. Retains the central wishbone chimney, liegender Stuhl truss, vaulted cellar, five-plate jamb stove and stone kitchen sink — the most legible surviving section of the type.
exemplars.why: The most legible section in the tradition - wishbone chimney, liegender Stuhl, vaulted cellar, five-plate jamb stove all surviving - which is SAH ARCHIPEDIA's list, not the government's; a National Historic Landmark since 2017, and the Department of the Interior's citation as Preservation Maryland quotes it puts the case more generally: 'an outstanding example of a Georgian-period house influenced by German American cultural and construction traditions'. CORRECTED 5 Sep 2026 by the cluster audit: the why had said the Landmark was designated 'on precisely that ground, per the Department of the Interior's own citation', and the citation names none of the four features.

exemplars.name: Heinrich Zeller House (Fort Zeller)
exemplars.note: Limestone house banked over an everflowing spring that discharges through an arched cellar opening; narrow irregular windows.
exemplars.why: The limestone country's own building and the one the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission names in its field-guide entry on the fortified Pennsylvania German house; carried here for the walls and openings rather than for the bank, which is pennsylvania-bank-house's business.

exemplars.name: House of Miller at Millbach
exemplars.location: Millbach, Millcreek Township, Lebanon County, Pennsylvania
exemplars.note: A 2 1/2-storey sandstone and limestone house with a gambrel roof, bell-cast at the base of each slope, and pent eaves crossing the GABLE ENDS rather than the facade; a datestone over the south entrance reads 'Jerg Muler/Maria. Catr. U/ 1752' in Rhineland dialect. Two interiors were removed in 1926 and are period rooms at the Philadelphia Museum of Art. The attached mill is dated 1784 by HABS and 1778 by a mill gazetteer.
exemplars.why: The HABS survey's own brief statement of significance calls it 'one of the finest and best known examples ... of Pennsylvania-German architecture', and its kitchen has been on display in a major museum since 1926, which is as close to a canon as this tradition has.

exemplars.name: Bethlehem Gemeinhaus
exemplars.location: 62-66 West Church Street, Bethlehem, Northampton County, Pennsylvania
exemplars.note: Built of white oak timbers in two stages 1741-43, with a two-storey attic over a partial cellar and a steep roof with kicked eaves; believed to be the largest eighteenth-century log structure in continuous use in the United States, and since 2024 part of the Moravian Church Settlements World Heritage site. The HABS item (PA-1142) is photographs only and its data page carries no written description.
exemplars.why: The Moravian branch of the tradition at institutional scale, and the one surviving building that shows the steep kicked-eave roof and the usable two-storey loft this node's description claims for the liegender Stuhl; the significance judgment is UNESCO's and the National Historic Landmark programme's, not this project's.

exemplars.name: Troxell-Steckel House
exemplars.location: 4229 Reliance Street, Egypt, Whitehall Township, Lehigh County, Pennsylvania
exemplars.note: A 2 1/2-storey fieldstone dwelling of 1756 with a high-pitched gable roof, 48 ft long by 35 ft wide, with a dated German inscription on the second storey and a separate contributing stone springhouse - the spring served from a building of its own rather than run through the cellar. The dimensions reach this record through Wikipedia's summary of the nomination, not through a survey.
exemplars.why: Plain and measurable, and useful as the control case for the bank house: same tradition, same decade, same limestone country, and the spring is a separate building instead of a floor of the dwelling.

exemplars.name: Bertolet-Herbein Cabin
exemplars.note: A one-and-a-half-storey log cabin of about 20 by 30 ft with a large stone chimney slightly off centre, two Dutch half doors on opposite sides, three double-hung windows and a steep gable roof that flares at the lower third. HABS in 1960 called it 'a simple and picturesque type of home built by the first settlers in the Pennsylvania-German country' and said it was in imminent danger of demolition. Its own survey disagrees with itself about whether the plan is two rooms or three.
exemplars.why: The log channel of this tradition, and the only building in the node whose HABS sheet is a full Part II description room by room -- openings, roof, chimney, plan, stairway, finishes and heating, where the stone houses are recorded on a one-page Architectural Data Form; the record was already in the corpus for log-vernacular-american, and the central chimney and the Germanic three-room reading make it this node's building as much as that one's. CORRECTED 5 Sep 2026 by the cluster audit: this had read 'fully measured by HABS where the stone houses are not', and the Hans Herr House and the Golden Plough Tavern both carry HABS plan dimensions in this same node.

sources: Sally McMurry and Nancy Van Dolsen, eds., Architecture and Landscape of the Pennsylvania Germans, 1720–1920 (2011)
Robert C. Bucher, 'The Continental Log House', Pennsylvania Folklife (1962)
Dell Upton and John Michael Vlach, eds., Common Places: Readings in American Vernacular Architecture (1986)
Bernard L. Herman and Gabrielle Lanier, Everyday Architecture of the Mid-Atlantic (1997)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)

proportion_packs.note: The canonical construction — squared limestone or sandstone, 18-30 in, with oversized dressed quoins 1.5 to 2.5 times the height of the field coursing — is a direct match to brick-course's own corner_quoin rule that quoins must be laid up in whole-course multiples so long and short faces alternate. german-pennsylvania-colonial is named directly in the pack's own applies_to. Bound primary, not merely optional, because stone is this style's canonical and most-cited walling: Hans Herr House, Schifferstadt and Fort Zeller are all stone exemplars.

Governs the log Einraumhaus of first settlement, listed as a 'common' massing affinity (hall-single-cell) and explicit in the style's own lineage as a hybridization with Scandinavian log construction — 'the Germans adopted it, added V- and dovetail-notching and their own three-room plan.' german-pennsylvania-colonial is named directly in log-module's own applies_to. Bound optional and second because the style's canonical, most-documented built form is the stone Flurküchenhaus, not the log cabin, but the log phase is real, dated (first settlement, pre-stone) and should not be dropped.

german-pennsylvania-colonial is named directly in the pack's own applies_to. The style's own governing_logic is close to a paraphrase of this pack's argument: 'a kitchen bay of 16-20 ft and a stove-room/chamber bay of the same total width' — a plan sized by function (the jamb-stove wall, the hearth) rather than by a treatise ratio.

The style's own constraint c05 restates sash-light's dated light-count logic almost verbatim: 'small casements... to c.1760; nine-over-six sash c.1760-1800; six-over-six after.' Bound for that dating arithmetic only. The style's own typical_ratios give a window opening ratio 'near 1:1.6' — squarer than sash-light's 1.85-2.6 measured Anglo-American band, and consistent with the style's own diagnostic tell that openings are 'placed by interior need rather than by facade composition.' Do not read sash-light's ratio figure onto this style's windows. opening-proportion was considered and rejected for the same reason, more strongly: its Palladian door-and-window derivation assumes a composed elevation, and this style's own diagnostic tell is that 'windows that do not line up floor to floor, in a house otherwise carefully built' show 'the plan... winning the argument with the elevation.'
